accuracy.evidence: Word meanings checked against the Cambridge Dictionary entries for jealous (wanting what someone else has), embarrassed, guilty and lonely. The scared-now versus worried-later split follows the APA Dictionary of Psychology, which separates fear (present-oriented, a specific threat) from anxiety and worry (future-oriented). Mixed feelings in this age group follow Larsen, To and Fireman (2007), who found older children aged 5 to 12 more likely to feel happy and sad at once; the RULER claim is stated as the paper reports it (higher grades and teacher-rated social skills, Brackett et al. 2012).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the mistakes named for this topic and age: one big word for every size of feeling (furious for a tapped chair), confusing close words (guilty for embarrassed, scared for a test next week), thinking alone always means lonely, believing you can only feel one thing at a time, and settling for blurry sad. Each has its own feedback line in the lab and challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are about word precision, not face reading or calming down: a strength thermometer that rejects a wrong order and names which end is off, a pair sorter whose bins show the separating clue (now or later, wanting company, doing wrong or being seen), a two-layer feeling jar, a multi-select for one event, and an I feel bubble. The distinctness gate passed against Naming Basic Emotions, Words for Big Feelings and Feelings Change and Differ.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children discover the ideas by acting: a wrong thermometer order is cleared with the reason, a misplaced card bounces with the clue for that pair, wrong jar words explain why they do not fit the moment, proud and grateful in Mia's party turn red with a reason while sad turns amber as true but blurry. Each finished step states the rule in one sentence.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: that annoyed and furious both just mean angry, that you cannot feel lonely in a busy playground, and that you can only feel one feeling at a time. The thermometer, the lonely card and the two-layer jar then show the answer, and the reveal quotes the child's pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating scenarios (a friend's new bike, feeding the cat unasked, alone at lunch, results next week, a tapped chair, letting a brother take the blame), each wrong option mapped to a specific reason, for example 'Guilty is for doing something wrong. Feeding the cat was a good thing.' and 'Furious is the very strongest anger. Match the size of the word to the size of the feeling.'

readability.evidence: Kid text scores Flesch-Kincaid grade 2.8 (family limit 5.0) and adult text 8.6 (limit 10); sentences are short and every new word comes with a plain meaning. Lab cards are one or two short sentences, and the young class gives larger buttons and text.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler. Each kid paragraph covers one evidence statement from the topic (wider words, strength, close cousins, proud, grateful, guilty, embarrassed and mixed feelings); the adult text gives the research basis, what the lab does, four named mistakes and one routine for home.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px Android light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots before and after Show me at every step. The first version squeezed embarrassed into a three-column tile, so the I feel choices were moved to full-width stacked tiles. Thermometer, pair cards, jar and party words stay readable, and every canvas target has a 56 px button twin below.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The canvas aria-label and live status line read the state ('Thermometer, mild to strong: step 1 annoyed...', 'Jar holds: excited and nervous'), every drag also works as tap-then-tap and as a labelled button, and reduced motion shortens the demo timing.
